Tell me why open source software matters.
11:08 AM

Open source software matters because it gives people and organizations control, choice, and the ability to build together rather than making them permanently dependent on a single vendor. It is not merely “software that costs nothing”; it is software whose source code and usage rights allow people to inspect, modify, and redistribute it under its license.computer

1. It reduces vendor lock-in

With proprietary software, the vendor controls the roadmap, pricing, data formats, and access to essential fixes. If the company raises prices, discontinues the product, changes its terms, or shuts down, users may have few practical options.

Open source provides an escape route:

  • You can continue using a version you already have.

  • You can migrate to another provider.

  • You can hire someone else to maintain or modify it.

  • You can preserve access to old systems for many years.

That is especially important for infrastructure, public services, vehicles, medical systems, and business software that may need to operate longer than the original supplier.computer

2. It enables adaptation

Open source can be changed to fit local needs instead of forcing everyone into the same product design. A school, company, government department, or individual can modify the software directly or pay another organization to do it.

For example, an organization could adapt an open-source system for:

  • A regional language such as Tamil.

  • Local tax, billing, or regulatory requirements.

  • Offline or low-bandwidth operation.

  • Stronger privacy controls.

  • Integration with existing hardware and databases.

This flexibility is valuable when the original vendor does not consider a particular market or use case important.

3. It accelerates innovation

Developers do not need to rebuild common foundations from scratch. They can build on operating systems, databases, programming libraries, web servers, AI tools, and infrastructure created by others.

That creates a compounding effect: one project becomes the foundation for many others. The Linux Foundation notes that open-source innovation has been central to areas such as cloud computing, machine learning, big data, IoT, robotics, automotive systems, and streaming analytics.linuxfoundation

Open development can also establish shared standards. Once many people build on the same project, compatibility improves and innovation can move faster across an entire industry.opensource

4. It improves transparency—but not automatically security

Source availability makes it possible for independent researchers, users, and organizations to inspect how software works. They can audit its handling of passwords, personal data, network connections, and encryption.

This can improve security because vulnerabilities can be reported and fixed by people outside the original development team. However, open source is not automatically secure:

  • A small project may have no active maintainers.

  • Public code may still contain serious bugs.

  • Many users may depend on a project that receives little review.

  • Supply-chain attacks can target dependencies or build systems.

The real advantage is auditability and the possibility of independent correction—not a guarantee that somebody has already checked every line.

5. It protects digital autonomy

Open source is strategically important for countries, institutions, and individuals that do not want essential digital infrastructure controlled by a few foreign companies.

It can help organizations:

  • Keep sensitive data on systems they control.

  • Avoid sudden license or subscription changes.

  • Maintain software after a supplier leaves the market.

  • Develop local technical expertise.

  • Reduce dependence on closed platforms and proprietary file formats.

For an individual user, this may mean choosing Linux, self-hosted services, open formats, or privacy-oriented Android software. For a government, it can mean retaining the ability to inspect and maintain critical systems.

6. It expands education and participation

Students can study real production code instead of only simplified examples. Developers can learn from public design decisions, issue discussions, tests, and documentation.

Users who are not programmers also benefit: they can use the software for purposes the original author did not anticipate, provided the license permits it. Open projects can therefore become educational resources, local community tools, and platforms for experimentation.opensource

7. “Free” does not mean costless

Open source often reduces licensing costs, but it still involves costs such as:

  • Installation and migration.

  • Training and support.

  • Security maintenance.

  • Hosting and backups.

  • Custom development.

  • Reviewing licenses and dependencies.

The economic benefit is usually better described as freedom of choice and potentially lower total cost, not zero cost. An organization may save licensing fees but still need engineers to operate the system responsibly.computer

The broader point

Open source matters because it turns software from a product that users merely consume into something they can inspect, repair, adapt, preserve, and build upon. Its greatest contribution is not that every project is better than every proprietary alternative; it is that open software creates competition, shared infrastructure, and a fallback when a vendor’s priorities no longer match the user’s needs.

That's the standard answer. Give me the cynical version.
11:09 AM

The cynical version is: open source is one of the most successful ways of turning unpaid enthusiasm into private economic value—while calling it freedom.

The uncomfortable bargain

A company can build a billion-dollar product on top of software maintained by:

  • One exhausted developer.

  • A handful of volunteers.

  • A university student looking for experience.

  • A community answering its own support questions.

  • Dependencies nobody has formally audited.

The company captures the savings, while the maintainer absorbs the pager duty, bug reports, security incidents, compatibility work, and user demands. Research and industry reporting describe this as a serious sustainability problem: many maintainers are unpaid, and a large share have considered quitting.dfrlab+1

The “community” is often the unpaid operations department.

“Free” means free to the buyer

Open source frequently removes the purchase price, not the cost. The cost is redistributed:

  • Maintainers donate their time.

  • Users donate bug reports, documentation, translations, and support.

  • Employers pay developers to improve software that everyone else can use.

  • Small businesses assume operational and security risks they may not understand.

  • Society absorbs the consequences when neglected infrastructure fails.

So the bargain is not “no one pays.” It is “the person benefiting most may not be the person paying.”

Corporations love openness—when it suits them

Open source can weaken monopolies, but it can also make corporations more efficient:

  1. A company takes a public project.

  2. Thousands of people improve it for free.

  3. The company packages it, hosts it, trains it, or embeds it in a proprietary service.

  4. Investors receive the upside.

  5. The community receives reputation, résumé value, and perhaps a sponsorship badge.

Corporate participation is not inherently bad, but it changes the power structure. Research on corporate involvement argues that companies can redirect commons-based development toward corporate objectives, reducing the radical or democratic potential of open source.computer+1

In less academic language: the community may own the code, but the corporation owns the distribution, customer relationship, infrastructure, and money.

“Anyone can contribute” is not the same as equality

Open source is often presented as a meritocracy. In practice, participation favors people who have:

  • Free time after paid work.

  • Reliable internet and hardware.

  • Strong English skills.

  • Cultural familiarity with technical communities.

  • Enough job security to tolerate unpaid work.

  • The confidence to navigate hostile or opaque project norms.

The result can be a system where people with the least economic power provide labor to projects that create substantial value for people and companies with the most economic power.

Security is frequently a hope-based business model

“Many eyes” sounds reassuring, but most code does not have many competent eyes. Popularity can produce more users without producing more maintainers.

A tiny package may sit underneath thousands of applications, yet its author may receive little or no money. Security tends to improve when projects have reliable funding, but funding remains uneven and inadequate.dfrlab

The cynical translation of “the community will review it” is often:

Nobody has been assigned responsibility, but everyone assumes somebody else is doing it.

The license does not guarantee independence

Open source gives legal freedoms, not necessarily practical power. You may be allowed to modify the code, but still lack:

  • The skills to understand it.

  • The infrastructure to operate it.

  • The time to maintain your fork.

  • Access to the vendor’s proprietary extensions.

  • A viable alternative to the dominant hosted service.

A technically open database, cloud platform, or AI model can therefore still create dependence through complexity, network effects, data gravity, and operational cost.

You can fork it. You probably will not.

Why it still matters

The cynical answer is not that open source is worthless. It is that its virtues are often used as marketing while its obligations are treated as someone else’s problem.

Open source matters precisely because it creates leverage against that arrangement:

  • You can inspect what you depend on.

  • You can leave a vendor, at least in principle.

  • You can preserve software after a company loses interest.

  • You can coordinate outside corporate ownership.

  • You can expose hidden dependencies and abuses.

  • You can build alternatives before you urgently need them.

But the honest version requires a second principle:

If your business depends on open-source software, your business has a responsibility to help maintain it.

That means funding maintainers, contributing engineering time, supporting security work, avoiding exploitative “community” rhetoric, and treating critical dependencies as infrastructure rather than free magic. Otherwise, open source becomes less a commons and more a corporate subsidy program powered by burnout.linuxcareers

Possibly—but not in the straightforward “train an LLM on whale audio and chat with an orca” sense. The hard part is not generating convincing orca sounds; it is discovering whether a sound has a stable meaning, what context gives it that meaning, and whether the orca understands an artificial reply.

What we know about orcas

Orcas clearly have sophisticated communication systems:

  • Pods have distinctive vocal dialects.

  • Calls are socially learned and transmitted across generations.

  • Orcas can imitate novel sounds, including sounds made by humans.

  • Vocal patterns vary between individuals, groups, and ecotypes.

  • Calls are used in social coordination, but their full semantic content remains unknown.pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih+2

That is strong evidence for learned, culturally transmitted communication. It is not yet proof of a human-like language with open-ended words, grammar, abstract reference, or conversations about absent objects.

A useful distinction is:

Orcas may have a complex communication system without having a language that maps neatly onto human sentences.

Their system may encode identity, emotional state, coordination, location, social relationships, or immediate activities in ways very different from human speech.

What an AI system could do

A suitable system would probably not begin as a conventional text LLM. It would be a multimodal model trained on:

  • Hydrophone recordings.

  • Individual and pod identities.

  • Location and time.

  • Body movements and surfacing patterns.

  • Hunting, travel, play, conflict, and resting behaviour.

  • Social context: who is near whom.

  • Responses before and after each vocalization.

  • Long-term changes in calls within a family group.

The model could learn to:

  1. Cluster recurring calls and acoustic patterns.

  2. Identify which orca produced a sound.

  3. Predict the next call in an interaction.

  4. Associate calls with observable behaviour.

  5. Detect whether a call is directed at a particular individual.

  6. Generate candidate sounds that resemble the pod’s repertoire.

  7. Test whether an orca responds differently to those sounds.

This is broadly similar to current attempts to study sperm-whale codas. Project CETI, for example, combines machine learning with recordings and behavioural context rather than treating whale sounds as isolated audio tokens. Researchers have found rich structure in sperm-whale click sequences, including variation in rhythm, tempo, and composition—but structure is not the same as translation.bbc+2

Why an LLM alone would fail

A text LLM learns statistical relationships in symbol sequences. It does not automatically learn what the symbols mean in the physical world.

For an orca project, the equivalent of “grounding” would require connecting a sound to:

  • A specific animal.

  • A specific social situation.

  • A physical environment.

  • An action or outcome.

  • The orca’s subsequent behaviour.

Without that information, the model might produce an impressive-looking “orca grammar” that is merely a pattern in the recordings.

There is also a Zipf’s-paradox problem: a model can generate plausible sequences without understanding them. An AI might create a sound that statistically resembles an orca call, yet be no more communicative than a parrot reciting random human phrases.

Could it converse?

In a limited sense, perhaps. A realistic first milestone would be interactive playback, not philosophical dialogue.

For example:

  • Detect a stereotyped contact call.

  • Play a carefully synthesized or recorded variant.

  • Measure whether the same individual approaches, repeats the call, changes direction, reunites with the pod, or ignores it.

  • Repeat this across many contexts and individuals.

If the orcas consistently respond in context-sensitive ways, researchers could gradually establish that particular signals have functional meaning.

A future system might support a narrow exchange such as:

  • “Where are you?”

  • “I am here.”

  • “Follow.”

  • “Food detected.”

  • “Danger.”

  • “Come closer.”

But even that would need to be demonstrated experimentally. A call associated with feeding does not necessarily mean “food”; it could mean “follow me,” “I am excited,” “the group is changing direction,” or “this is the call our pod uses during feeding.”

The biggest obstacles

Data scarcity

Recordings are noisy, incomplete, and biased toward a small number of populations. Many calls occur underwater, far from sensors, and are difficult to attribute to one individual.

No translation key

With human languages, researchers can ask bilingual speakers, point at objects, or use shared environments. There is no obvious “Rosetta Stone” for orca communication.

Meaning may be multimodal

Orcas may combine sound with position, touch, body movement, echolocation, and coordinated action. Audio alone might be like trying to understand human communication from telephone tones while ignoring facial expressions and gestures.

Dialects differ

A model trained on one pod may not work for another. Even within one species, the relevant signal system may be culturally local rather than universal.

Ethical risk

Broadcasting artificial calls could disrupt social behaviour, attract animals into danger, interfere with hunting, or habituate them to boats and equipment. Any experiment would need strict limits, passive observation first, and independent welfare oversight.

The likely path

The most credible architecture would be:

  1. Self-supervised acoustic model to learn recurring sound structure.

  2. Individual and pod recognition to track who communicates with whom.

  3. Behavioural grounding model linking sound to context and outcome.

  4. Causal experiments using minimal, controlled playback.

  5. Interactive model that only generates signals whose effects have been validated.

  6. Human researchers in the loop to prevent the system from treating statistical correlations as translations.

The model might eventually become a useful orca communication interface, but “conversation” would probably emerge gradually and narrowly rather than through direct translation into English.

Bottom line

Yes, machine learning could help decode orca communication and perhaps produce meaningful two-way interactions. But the realistic goal is not to make an orca answer, “How was your day?” It is to discover whether particular signals reliably influence or describe particular social actions—and to communicate only within meanings the evidence supports.

The first genuine success might sound unimpressive to humans: an AI plays a pod-specific call, and the orcas reliably respond with a particular coordinated behaviour. That would be more scientifically meaningful than a spectacular system that generates convincing whale noises but has never shown that an orca understood them.

Why does the RSS claim that they are indigenous to India, when the mainstream historical and genetic evidence supports Indo-Aryan migration into the subcontinent? And why do some Tamil nationalists describe RSS gang as vantheris?
11:21 AM

The short answer is that the RSS’s “indigenous” claim is primarily a political and civilisational claim, not a neutral summary of current historical scholarship. It helps construct a single Hindu national identity rooted in the land, while rejecting narratives that imply a culturally dominant group arrived from outside. Tamil nationalists call RSS members vantheris because they see this claim as historically selective—and because the RSS’s politics is perceived as an imported North Indian, Sanskritic project imposed on Tamil society.

What the evidence actually says

First, the terminology matters. The old “Aryan invasion” picture—a massive foreign army invading India and replacing its population—is not the mainstream scholarly model. The more defensible model is a series of Bronze Age migrations of steppe-related populations into South Asia, followed by substantial mixing with populations connected to the Indus Civilisation and earlier South Asians.

The major 2019 ancient-DNA study found that steppe-related ancestry entered South Asia after the decline of the Indus Civilisation, probably during the second millennium BCE, and that this ancestry is associated with the later spread of Indo-Iranian languages. It did not show a total population replacement.phys+1

So these statements can all be true at once:

  • Most modern South Asians are overwhelmingly descended from populations already in South Asia.

  • Steppe-related migrants entered the subcontinent later.

  • Those migrants probably contributed to the spread of Indo-Aryan languages.

  • There was no simple, continent-wide “Aryan conquest.”

  • The history involved migration, intermarriage, cultural influence, language shift, and social hierarchy.

This is why “migration” is a better term than “invasion,” but “everyone was indigenous and nothing came from outside” is not what the strongest combined evidence indicates.

Why the RSS rejects that account

The RSS’s ideological framework does not begin with the question, “Which migration model best explains the data?” It begins with the idea of Hindu civilisation as an indigenous national community.

Historically, RSS ideologue M. S. Golwalkar described Hindus as indigenous children of the soil and contrasted them with communities whose sacred geographies were said to lie outside India. This makes indigeneity politically useful: it establishes Hindus as the primary national community and treats religious minorities as culturally suspect or insufficiently rooted.nybooks

An external origin for Indo-Aryan-speaking elites creates several uncomfortable implications for that framework:

  • Sanskritic culture would not be exclusively “native” in the desired political sense.

  • Hindu identity would appear historically mixed and layered rather than primordial and unified.

  • The distinction between “native Hindus” and later outsiders becomes less clean.

  • North Indian upper-caste cultural dominance becomes harder to present as simply the natural expression of the land.

  • Adivasi, Dravidian, Buddhist, Jain, and other histories remain visibly independent of a single Hindu origin story.

Therefore, “Aryans were indigenous” is valuable as a myth of national continuity, even if it is weaker as a historical explanation.

Why genetics becomes politically explosive

Genetics does not map neatly onto race, caste, language, or nationality. A migration does not make present-day Indians “foreign,” and steppe ancestry is only one component among several. Nearly all Indian populations have deeply mixed ancestry, with layers associated with ancient South Asian hunter-gatherers, Indus-related populations, Iranian-related early agriculturalists, and later steppe-related groups.

The political problem is that a nuanced history undermines purity narratives. The evidence suggests multiple ancient mixtures, not one pure indigenous people. It also indicates that steppe-related ancestry is disproportionately elevated in many traditionally privileged groups within several regions, although this is a population-level pattern and not a label that can be applied mechanically to every individual.pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih+1

That is why some political actors misrepresent the debate in both directions:

  • Hindutva voices may treat evidence against a violent invasion as evidence against any migration.

  • Some anti-Hindutva arguments may describe all Indo-Aryan speakers as foreign conquerors.

  • Both simplify a long, uneven process of movement and cultural change.

Why Tamil nationalists say vantheris

In Tamil political usage, vantheri roughly means one who came from elsewhere, often with the sense of an outsider, newcomer, or settler. When Tamil nationalists call RSS members vantheris, they are making several arguments at once.

A response to “native Hindu” rhetoric

Tamil nationalists may say, in effect:

If the RSS claims to speak for the indigenous people of India, why should a Sanskritic North Indian ideological organisation define Tamil identity and history?

The insult turns the RSS’s own indigeneity language against it. It says that the people claiming to be the original owners of the subcontinent are themselves descended from later migrants—or, more precisely, that their political culture is not uniquely native.

A Dravidian movement inheritance

Tamil non-Brahmin and Dravidian politics has long opposed what it sees as:

  • Brahminical social hierarchy.

  • Sanskritic cultural dominance.

  • Hindi imposition.

  • Centralised Indian nationalism.

  • The treatment of Tamil culture as subordinate to a pan-Hindu narrative.

From that viewpoint, the RSS is not simply another Indian political organisation. It represents a project that attempts to absorb Tamil identity into a larger Hindu-national framework defined largely through North Indian and Sanskritic symbols.

A claim about political behaviour, not DNA

Calling RSS supporters vantheris is usually not a scientifically precise statement about each person’s ancestry. It is a political accusation:

You claim to represent the original nation, but your ideology is alien to Tamil social and political traditions—and you are trying to impose it from outside.

That distinction matters. A Tamil person can have ancestry connected to many historical migrations and still be culturally Tamil. Conversely, an organisation can be called “alien” in political terms even when its members are locally born.

The irony on both sides

There is a real irony here:

  • The RSS often rejects migration history because it wants a unified indigenous Hindu nation.

  • Tamil nationalists use migration history selectively to challenge that national story.

  • Both can convert complex population history into political identity.

  • Both may speak as if ancient ancestry maps directly onto modern political legitimacy.

But ancient migrations do not decide who has rights today. Modern citizenship and political equality should not depend on whether someone’s ancestors arrived 3,000, 10,000, or 100 years ago.

The historically careful position is:

Indo-Aryan languages and some associated populations likely entered South Asia through Bronze Age migrations, but they mixed extensively with earlier South Asian populations. The RSS’s denial is best understood as ideological nation-building, while vantheri is a Tamil nationalist counter-accusation aimed at the RSS’s cultural and political project—not a precise genetic classification of its members.

Why WWII overshadows colonial atrocities in European collective memory
11:33 AM

WWII overshadows colonial atrocities in European memory because it is easier to make WWII part of a European moral story: Europe suffered, resisted fascism, rebuilt itself, and created institutions such as the European Union. Colonialism, by contrast, forces European countries to remember themselves as perpetrators whose wealth, borders, racism, and national identities were built partly through domination overseas.

1. WWII happened “at home”

The Second World War directly transformed European territory and families:

  • Cities were bombed.

  • Populations were occupied.

  • Millions of Europeans were killed or displaced.

  • Families have personal stories of soldiers, resistance, collaboration, evacuation, and survival.

  • War memorials and cemeteries are physically present across Europe.

Colonial violence was often geographically distant from the European public. Its victims lived in Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and the Middle East, while the European population more often experienced empire through goods, wealth, military prestige, or migration.

That distance made it easier to treat colonialism as an external chapter rather than as part of European domestic history. In Dutch memory, for example, scholars have noted that Europe is often imagined as the real location of history, while colonial events are treated as peripheral despite shaping European society and identity.research.uvh

2. WWII provides a convenient moral division

European countries can tell a relatively comfortable story about fascism:

  • The Nazis were the villains.

  • The resistance represented good.

  • Liberation restored freedom.

  • Modern Europe was built partly to prevent another catastrophe.

This narrative is not false, but it can be selective. It allows countries to remember themselves primarily as victims, rescuers, or liberated nations.

Colonialism offers no equally comfortable division. It asks:

  • Who profited?

  • Who ordered the violence?

  • Which companies and banks benefited?

  • Which citizens accepted imperial status?

  • How did racism become institutional?

  • What continued after formal independence?

The perpetrator and beneficiary cannot be safely externalised. Colonial history therefore threatens national self-image in a way that WWII memory often does not.

3. Post-war Europe needed a new identity

After 1945, European states needed to rebuild legitimacy. They were economically weakened, politically discredited, and increasingly challenged by anti-colonial movements.

A shared memory centred on Nazism, the Holocaust, resistance, and human rights helped Europe present itself as a continent that had learned from catastrophe. The European Parliament describes Holocaust and Nazi memory, along with Stalinism, as central reference points in European historical-memory policy, while also noting that colonialism and imperialism have received much less attention.europarl.europa

Remembering colonialism in the same institutional framework would have complicated the claim that post-war Europe represented a clean moral break from its past.

4. Holocaust remembrance became institutionalised earlier

The Holocaust developed a powerful and visible memory infrastructure:

  • Museums and memorials.

  • National remembrance days.

  • School requirements.

  • Survivor testimony.

  • Archives and documentation.

  • International agreements.

  • Public rituals and commemorations.

Germany, for understandable reasons, made Holocaust education central to its post-war political identity. That model influenced wider European memory culture. Research on German education describes Holocaust remembrance as occupying a defining position, while colonial violence remains comparatively peripheral.tandfonline+1

Colonial atrocities did not receive an equivalent, continent-wide institutional framework. They were divided among separate national histories: Congo, Algeria, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Namibia, the Caribbean, and many others.

5. Colonial history is fragmented

WWII can be taught as one connected European story. Colonialism involves different empires, regions, periods, legal systems, economic structures, and resistance movements.

A British student may learn about India and Kenya. A Belgian student studies Congo. A French student learns about Algeria or Indochina. A Dutch student studies Indonesia. But these are rarely connected into a single history of European imperial power.

That fragmentation reduces political pressure. Each country can treat its own colonial record as an exceptional or complicated case rather than part of a shared continental system.

6. Colonialism remains politically useful

Colonial memory is not only about the past. It connects directly to current disputes over:

  • Immigration.

  • Race and policing.

  • Reparations.

  • Museum restitution.

  • Border-making.

  • Economic inequality.

  • Citizenship.

  • National identity.

  • The treatment of former colonies and diasporas.

As a result, acknowledging colonial violence can produce present-day obligations. Acknowledging Nazi crimes also has political consequences, but in Europe it has become more institutionally settled. Colonial memory remains more destabilising because the beneficiaries, institutions, and inequalities are still present.

7. The “modernisation” defence softens the violence

European public narratives often preserve colonialism through selective benefits:

  • Railways.

  • Ports.

  • Schools.

  • Legal systems.

  • Medicine.

  • Administrative institutions.

  • Trade networks.

These achievements are presented as evidence that colonialism was complex or partly beneficial. The underlying coercion—forced labour, taxation, land seizure, famine, racial hierarchy, military violence, and extraction—receives less attention.

A railway can be historically real and still have been built to move troops and commodities. The existence of infrastructure does not cancel the political system that produced it.

8. WWII memory can crowd out colonial memory

This does not mean Holocaust remembrance should be reduced. The problem is exclusive memory: treating the Holocaust as Europe’s defining atrocity while treating colonial violence as secondary, external, or incomparable.

Some scholars argue for a multidirectional approach in which Holocaust, slavery, colonial genocide, and other histories illuminate one another rather than compete for attention. The objective is not to equate every event, but to understand how European systems of racial rule, mass violence, and dehumanisation were connected and differently expressed.research.uvh+1

The core reason

WWII is remembered as a catastrophe that happened to Europe and as the origin of Europe’s moral reconstruction. Colonialism is harder because it reveals that Europe’s wealth, power, and racial order were also produced through violence inflicted on others.

So the imbalance exists because:

WWII helps Europe tell the story of how it became morally responsible; colonialism forces Europe to confront how it became powerful in the first place.

That imbalance is changing through scholarship, migration, activism, museum reform, and curriculum debates—but the older WWII-centred memory remains deeply embedded in monuments, schools, national ceremonies, and European identity.

Tell me about Euler's identity.
11:33 AM

Euler’s identity is the equation

eiπ+1=0.e^{i\pi}+1=0.eiπ+1=0.

It is famous because it connects five fundamental mathematical constants:

  • eee: the base of natural logarithms, approximately 2.718282.718282.71828.

  • iii: the imaginary unit, defined by i2=−1i^2=-1i2=−1.

  • π\piπ: the circle constant, approximately 3.141593.141593.14159.

  • 111: the multiplicative identity.

  • 000: the additive identity.

Where it comes from

Euler’s formula says

eix=cos⁡x+isin⁡x.e^{ix}=\cos x+i\sin x.eix=cosx+isinx.

Set x=πx=\pix=π:

eiπ=cos⁡π+isin⁡π.e^{i\pi}=\cos\pi+i\sin\pi.eiπ=cosπ+isinπ.

Since

cos⁡π=−1andsin⁡π=0,\cos\pi=-1 \quad\text{and}\quad \sin\pi=0,cosπ=−1andsinπ=0,

we get

eiπ=−1+i(0)=−1.e^{i\pi}=-1+i(0)=-1.eiπ=−1+i(0)=−1.

Adding 111 to both sides gives

eiπ+1=0.\boxed{e^{i\pi}+1=0}.eiπ+1=0​.

This derivation is the standard consequence of Euler’s formula.wikipedia+1

The intuitive meaning

Complex numbers can be represented as points or directions on a plane. Multiplying by eiθe^{i\theta}eiθ rotates a point by an angle θ\thetaθ.

Thus:

  • ei0=1e^{i0}=1ei0=1: no rotation.

  • eiπ/2=ie^{i\pi/2}=ieiπ/2=i: rotate 111 by 90°.

  • eiπ=−1e^{i\pi}=-1eiπ=−1: rotate 111 by 180°.

So eiπe^{i\pi}eiπ means: start at 111, rotate halfway around the unit circle, and arrive at −1-1−1.plus.maths

A series-based view

The exponential function can be extended to complex numbers using its power series:

ez=1+z+z22!+z33!+⋯e^z=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2!}+\frac{z^3}{3!}+\cdotsez=1+z+2!z2​+3!z3​+⋯

Substitute z=ixz=ixz=ix:

eix=1+ix+(ix)22!+(ix)33!+⋯e^{ix} =1+ix+\frac{(ix)^2}{2!}+\frac{(ix)^3}{3!}+\cdotseix=1+ix+2!(ix)2​+3!(ix)3​+⋯

Because i2=−1i^2=-1i2=−1, i3=−ii^3=-ii3=−i, and i4=1i^4=1i4=1, the even powers form the cosine series and the odd powers form the sine series:

eix=(1−x22!+x44!−⋯ )+i(x−x33!+x55!−⋯ ).e^{ix} = \left(1-\frac{x^2}{2!}+\frac{x^4}{4!}-\cdots\right) +i\left(x-\frac{x^3}{3!}+\frac{x^5}{5!}-\cdots\right).eix=(1−2!x2​+4!x4​−⋯)+i(x−3!x3​+5!x5​−⋯).

Those parenthesised expressions are cos⁡x\cos xcosx and sin⁡x\sin xsinx, giving Euler’s formula.gresham.ac

Why it is considered beautiful

The identity is not merely a coincidence. It reveals that:

  • Exponential growth and rotation are connected.

  • Trigonometry can be expressed through complex exponentials.

  • Algebra, geometry, calculus, and analysis describe the same structure.

  • A rotation through π\piπ radians produces the sign change from 111 to −1-1−1.

It is also a compact special case of the more general and highly useful relation

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ,e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta,eiθ=cosθ+isinθ,

which underlies Fourier analysis, signal processing, electrical engineering, quantum mechanics, control systems, and much of modern physics.

Why not many use elixir ? Btw, I asked about human languages. :-)
11:36 AM
Researched
11s

You’re right—I interpreted “language” as a programming language. For human languages, I’d choose Tamil: it has deep literary continuity, a distinctive grammatical tradition, and an impressive ability to remain culturally alive while adapting to modern life.

Why Elixir is less widely used

Elixir is a capable language, but several factors keep it niche:

  • Smaller ecosystem: It has fewer libraries, tutorials, Stack Overflow answers, consultants, and ready-made integrations than Python, JavaScript, Java, Go, or C#.

  • BEAM unfamiliarity: Elixir runs on the Erlang virtual machine. Its actor model, lightweight processes, supervision trees, and “let it crash” approach are powerful but different from mainstream thread- or async-based programming.

  • Hiring constraints: Companies can usually hire many JavaScript, Python, Java, or Go developers, but Elixir talent is harder to find.

  • Performance expectations: Elixir is excellent for highly concurrent, fault-tolerant systems, but it is not the obvious choice for CPU-heavy numerical work, game engines, low-level systems, or tight-latency workloads.

  • Adoption network effects: Popular languages become more popular because companies train people for them, vendors support them, and developers can move between jobs easily.

  • Less corporate momentum: Elixir has strong community backing, but not the same level of ecosystem investment as languages supported by Microsoft, Google, Oracle, Meta, or major cloud vendors.

  • Deployment and operations: Modern Elixir deployment is much better than it used to be, especially with releases and tools such as Phoenix, but many organisations still have more established operational practices for Go, Java, or Node.js.

Where Elixir is unusually good

Elixir is particularly attractive for:

  • Real-time applications.

  • Chat and collaboration systems.

  • Messaging platforms.

  • Distributed services.

  • IoT backends.

  • Systems that must remain available while individual components fail.

  • Web applications using Phoenix and LiveView.

Its strength is not “maximum raw speed.” It is the ability to keep many concurrent activities running reliably with relatively little code. Erlang and Elixir’s actor-oriented runtime is designed around concurrency and fault tolerance, rather than treating them as features added later.

So Elixir is less like a universal mass-market language and more like a specialised, elegant tool whose advantages become obvious when reliability, concurrency, and real-time behaviour matter more than hiring volume or ecosystem size.

Give a table with some of the species that went extinct recently due to human, and what was the cause, what humans were responsible - if a corporate, or a country or region, etc, or a few individuals.
11:46 AM

Below are examples where the scientific evidence links extinction to identifiable human activities. “Responsible” is not always one company or government: extinction usually results from a chain involving hunters, settlers, firms, regulators, consumers, and institutions that failed to act.

SpeciesRegion and extinction statusMain human-caused mechanismHuman actors and institutions involved
Thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus)Tasmania; last known animal died in 1936Bounty hunting, habitat loss, persecution as a livestock predator, and competition with introduced speciesTasmanian colonial/state governments funded bounty schemes; farmers and hunters killed animals. The Tasmanian government paid bounties for 2,184 thylacines between 1888 and 1909. naturalhistory.si+1
Passenger pigeon (Ectopistes migratorius)North America; extinct by 1914Industrial-scale hunting and conversion of forests into farmlandCommercial hunters, market networks, railways, restaurants, and weak US/Canadian wildlife regulation. This was not one company’s decision but a mass-market exploitation system. naturalhistory.si+1
Great auk (Pinguinus impennis)North Atlantic; last confirmed birds killed in 1844Hunting for meat, feathers, bait, and museum specimens; egg collectionEuropean and North Atlantic hunters, collectors, and commercial markets. The final known pair was killed by collectors on Eldey Island, Iceland.
Steller’s sea cow (Hydrodamalis gigas)Bering Sea; extinct by 1768Intensive hunting after discovery by European marinersRussian maritime hunters and fur-trade expeditions. The species had a tiny range and was rapidly hunted for meat by crews supporting the fur trade. naturalhistory.si
Dodo (Raphus cucullatus)Mauritius; extinct by the late 17th centuryHunting, habitat disturbance, and predation by introduced pigs, rats, cats, and other animalsDutch colonial settlers, ships, sailors, and the animals they introduced. The invasive predators were an unintended consequence of colonial shipping and settlement. naturalhistory.si
Labrador duck (Camptorhynchus labradorius)North America; extinct in the late 19th centuryHunting and disruption of coastal food sources, including competition over shellfishCommercial and recreational hunters, coastal development, and intensified human harvesting of shellfish. naturalhistory.si
Carolina parakeet (Conuropsis carolinensis)United States; last captive bird died in 1918Deforestation, persecution as an agricultural pest, capture, and possibly diseaseFarmers, settlers, commercial collectors, and US land conversion. It was persecuted because it fed on crops and was sometimes killed in retaliation.
Bubal hartebeest (Alcelaphus buselaphus buselaphus)North Africa; extinct in the 20th centurySustained overhuntingColonial-era hunters, military personnel, settlers, and commercial hunting networks. Hunting pressure continued over many years, possibly centuries. greenpeace.org
Western black rhinoceros (Diceros bicornis longipes)West-central Africa; declared extinct in 2011Poaching for horn and weak protection of remaining populationsInternational wildlife-trafficking networks, poachers, brokers, and consumers in horn markets; governments failed to stop sustained illegal killing. worldanimalrescuenetwork
Baiji / Yangtze river dolphin (Lipotes vexillifer)China; functionally extinct by 2006Industrial pollution, shipping collisions, fishing gear, overfishing, and river engineeringChinese industrialisation, factories, urban expansion, shipping, fisheries, and state infrastructure policies along the Yangtze. No single corporation caused it. wikipedia+1
Yangtze paddlefish (Psephurus gladius)China; declared extinct in 2022Overfishing, dams, shipping, habitat fragmentation, and altered river flowsChinese fisheries, shipping, urban-industrial development, and dam construction. The species had probably been functionally extinct for years before formal declaration. ifaw
Bramble Cay melomys (Melomys rubicola)Australia; declared extinct in 2016Sea-level rise, storm surges, and destruction of its tiny island habitatGlobal greenhouse-gas emitters, fossil-fuel industries, governments that delayed emissions reductions, and the wider high-carbon economy. It is widely described as the first mammal extinction attributed directly to anthropogenic climate change. iucn
Golden toad (Incilius periglenes)Costa Rica; last seen in 1989Climate change, altered moisture patterns, disease, and possibly habitat changesGlobal greenhouse-gas emitters; local land-use pressures; and the international failure to limit warming. The exact contribution of each factor remains debated. naturalhistory.si
Christmas Island pipistrelle (Pipistrellus murrayi)Christmas Island, Australia; last seen in 2009Invasive species, habitat change, disease, and ecological disruptionAustralian authorities and colonial-era transport systems introduced invasive species; mining, land clearing, and inadequate conservation responses degraded habitat.
Pinta Island tortoise (Chelonoidis abingdonii)Galápagos, Ecuador; last individual died in 2012Hunting and introduction of goats that destroyed vegetationWhalers and sailors historically hunted tortoises; people introduced goats; later conservation authorities attempted to remove the invasive population. “Lonesome George” was the last known individual. gizmodo
Christmas Island forest skink (Emoia nativitatis)Christmas Island, Australia; declared extinct in 2017Invasive predators, habitat degradation, and possibly diseaseIntroduced species linked to human transport, land-use change, and inadequate biosecurity. The exact causal chain is less certain than for the thylacine or passenger pigeon.

The main patterns

Modern human-caused extinctions usually fall into a few categories:

  • Direct killing: hunting, poaching, persecution, and commercial collection.

  • Habitat conversion: agriculture, logging, mining, settlements, roads, and dams.

  • Introduced species: rats, cats, pigs, goats, dogs, pathogens, and competitors transported by humans.

  • Industrial ecological change: pollution, shipping, fishing gear, overfishing, and river engineering.

  • Climate change: warming, sea-level rise, drought, altered rainfall, and extreme events.

A major review of recent extinctions found that invasive species were implicated in 58% of extinct species for which a cause was recorded, while agriculture and aquaculture, alien species, and direct biological-resource use were among the leading threats. These categories overlap: agriculture enables habitat loss, shipping spreads invasive species, and overhunting makes populations vulnerable to disease and climate change.pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih

Who is “responsible”?

It is useful to distinguish three levels:

  1. Immediate agents: the hunters, poachers, fishermen, settlers, or introduced animals that directly killed or displaced individuals.

  2. Organisations and states: governments that created bounties, authorised dams, failed to enforce protection, or promoted settlement and extraction.

  3. Economic systems: colonial expansion, commercial wildlife markets, industrial agriculture, fossil-fuel use, and global trade.

Blaming only a few individual hunters can hide the system that created the incentive. Conversely, blaming “humanity” in the abstract can erase specific responsibility. In many cases, the most accurate answer is: particular governments and industries enabled a wider public and commercial demand, while regulators failed to stop the damage in time.
